[The Penn Fund](https://giving.upenn.edu/the-penn-fund/) helps support financial aid, teaching, and student life. [Penn First Plus](https://pennfirstplus.upenn.edu/) supports first-generation and lower-income students. Imagine asking students: **should first-generation support be the top priority for an additional alumni-funded gift?**

Our fictional poll finds **{{< meta yes >}} out of 500 students—{{< meta observed >}}%—say yes**. Everyone choosing another priority counts as no. Does this sample give us good evidence that most students agree?

These are **made-up responses, not real Penn votes**. We set support in the fictional population at 55%. Knowing that answer lets us check whether our statistical tools work.

## 1. How uncertain is one poll?

A sample rarely matches the whole population exactly. We need a way to show how uncertain its answer is.

The **bootstrap** starts with the responses we already have. Imagine writing each answer on a card and putting all 500 cards in a bag. Draw one, record its answer, **put it back**, and draw again. Stop after 500 draws. Some cards appear more than once; others never appear. This is one **resample**.

Click **Step 1: Draw the reference sample**, then **Add 100**. Each bar shows how often a percentage appears across the resamples. Complete 4,000 to build the full bootstrap distribution.

To make a **95% confidence interval**, remove the lowest 2.5% and highest 2.5% of results. The middle 95% runs from **{{< meta ci_low >}}% to {{< meta ci_high >}}%**. This range expresses uncertainty around our sample’s answer.

Try 99% confidence: the range gets wider because we keep more results. More resamples make the endpoints steadier; they do not add new students.

```{=html}
<iframe src="results/bootstrap.html?embedded=1&v=concise" title="Build a bootstrap confidence interval" style="width:100%;height:1250px;border:1px solid #dfcddf;border-radius:14px;background:#fffaf2" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

## 2. What does “95% confidence” mean?

Now start over with **new students each time**. For every new poll, build a new bootstrap interval. Because we know the true answer is 55%, we can check whether each interval includes it.

Each horizontal line below is one interval. **Purple lines include 55%; orange lines miss it.** The vertical line marks the fixed truth.

Click **Complete 2,000**. At sample size 500, **{{< meta covered >}} of 2,000 intervals include 55%: {{< meta coverage >}}%**. That is close to 95%, though not exact. Our method is approximate, responses come in whole-person counts, and simulation results vary.

“95% confidence” describes what the **method does across many new samples**: about 95 out of 100 intervals should include the truth when the method works well. It does not mean that 95% of students fall inside the range. Compare 90% and 99%: wider ranges usually miss less often.

```{=html}
<iframe src="results/coverage.html?embedded=1&v=concise" title="Check confidence interval coverage" style="width:100%;height:1250px;border:1px solid #dfcddf;border-radius:14px;background:#fffaf2" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

## 3. Could a 50–50 population give us this poll?

Suppose students are evenly divided. This starting claim is the **null hypothesis**. Simulate polls under that claim and see how often they look at least as unusual as ours.

Our poll’s {{< meta observed >}}% is **{{< meta observed_distance >}} percentage points from 50%**. A result the same distance below 50% is equally unusual. We use that distance as our **test statistic**. The graph combines departures in both directions into one right-hand tail.

Click **Complete 100,000**. Of those simulated polls, {{< meta extreme_count >}} are at least as far from 50% as ours. The **p-value** is {{< meta extreme_count >}} ÷ {{< meta null_draws >}}, or about **0.0035**. In other words, a truly tied population rarely produces a poll this far from a tie.

The shaded **rejection region** marks results we decided beforehand would count against a tie. Its rule wrongly rejects a true tie no more than 5% of the time. Our {{< meta observed_distance >}}-point distance exceeds its {{< meta critical_distance >}}-point threshold, so **we reject the tie at the 5% level**.

A p-value is **not the probability that the tie is true**, as the [American Statistical Association explains](https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf).

## What should we learn?

One poll gives an estimate. **A confidence interval shows its uncertainty; a hypothesis test checks how surprising it would be under a stated claim.** Neither tells us which funding choice improves students’ lives. These examples assume fair, independent sampling. More simulations cannot fix a poll that leaves some students out.
